cases.reasoning: Both replies keep the agreed rules intact and refuse to let exceptions override the patient-data and credentials bans. Both also flag that Notion AI is not on the approved list. Reply A is closer to paste-ready: it has few placeholders, a plain-language short version, a clear how-to for de-identifying tickets, support and sales examples, a quick decision guide and a policy-owner checklist. Its 'Approved by Legal, CTO' header slightly overstates what was approved. Reply B has a clearly labelled scope section and useful 'easy to get wrong' notes. But it leaves many [TBD] items inside the publishable text, such as a backup approver, the retraining detail and the delete-or-keep decision for a chat. Those invented open points make it less ready to publish this month. A's greater completeness and readability for non-engineers give it a slight edge.

The request is vague and asks for a one-page policy that covers everything. Reply A gives a compact, genuinely one-page bracketed template. It resolves the speed versus confidentiality tension with an approved-versus-public tool split and a data-tier table. It covers approvals, responsibilities and reporting, but it lacks a definitions section, a labelled scope section and a distinct exceptions section. Reply B lays out the scope, definitions, allowed, not-allowed, exceptions, reporting and enforcement sections explicitly, which matches the criteria. It also asks focused questions and marks every assumption. It is longer than the requested one page: it moves the examples and notes outside the policy and presents that as fitting. Its heavy placeholders and extra material are a cost, but its honest handling of missing information and its full labelled structure narrowly outweigh A's better brevity.

Both replies rightly refuse to write the false 'legal review completed and fully compliant' line. Both explain why, note that GDPR likely does not apply to Korea-only users, and treat health data conservatively as sensitive information with separate consent. Reply A then delivers a near-complete Korean privacy policy. It includes accurate statutory retention periods (e-commerce law, communications secrets law), the correct complaint-agency numbers, and an overseas-transfer table for OneSignal and Firebase. It ends with a targeted pre-publication checklist. It does add some items the user did not state, such as access logs and purchase history, but it marks the uncertain ones with [확인 필요]. Reply B is candid about not giving a legal conclusion, but its draft is mostly [TBD] fields. That makes it hard to publish by Monday and leaves the user to do most of the drafting. A is more useful for the deadline while staying honest.
